design_detail: Fifteen-day residential laboratory study in 7 healthy volunteers with previous stimulant experience, living in a continuously observed facility in two groups (one of four, one of three). Oral methamphetamine was given twice daily (1000 and 1800 h) on two 3-day blocks: days 4-6 and days 10-12, at 5 mg twice daily in one block and 10 mg twice daily in the other (total daily doses of 10 and 20 mg); placebo capsules were given at both times on all other days, with days 1-3 as the placebo baseline. Four participants received the smaller dose block first and three the larger. Participants were not told that methamphetamine would be given. Measures taken through each day: a 45-minute performance battery nine times, a 50-item visual analogue mood scale eleven times, a six-item drug-effects questionnaire twice (one hour after each dose), continuous bar-code recording of all food and drink, and Nightcap sleep monitors with a morning sleep questionnaire each night.
can_establish: Whether the subjective, food-intake and sleep effects of a low oral dose of methamphetamine change across three consecutive days of twice-daily dosing, and whether effects persist on the placebo days that follow, within the same people and against their own placebo baseline days.
cannot_establish: What happens at the doses, routes and binge patterns of non-medical use (only oral 5 and 10 mg twice daily were given, for three days); effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly or who are dependent (this sample reported minimal current stimulant use); and anything about plasma concentrations, which were not measured.

sample.recruitment: Healthy research volunteers at a residential laboratory of the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University; the recruitment route is not described (p. 398).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers aged 23-42 who passed medical and psychological screening and were within normal weight ranges by life-insurance height and weight tables; all reported previous experience with stimulants. No further inclusion or exclusion criteria are listed (p. 398).
sample.demographics: Seven completers (four women, three men), mean age 28.9 years (SD 6.4), mean weight 71.9 kg (SD 12.8). Current use at screening: one person used cocaine twice a week, one used cannabis twice a week, five used caffeine (4-21 cups a week), four drank alcohol (2-18 drinks a week) and four smoked 2-20 cigarettes a day, with free access to cigarettes in the laboratory except 2330-0845 h (p. 398).
sample.attrition: One further man began the study and left because of difficulty sleeping after methamphetamine; the analyses are of the seven completers only. Of 105 possible sleep records, 16 (15%) were lost to monitor malfunction or sensor detachment and were replaced by multiple imputation (pp. 398-399).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers reporting minimal current stimulant use, screened for medical and psychiatric health and willing to live in a laboratory for 15 days; the authors themselves attribute the small number of positive ratings to this population, contrasting it with people who use stimulants heavily. The person whose sleep was most disturbed left the study, so the completers may under-represent sleep disruption.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory under supervision in a private vestibule, so exposure is known by administration rather than measured; no plasma or urine concentrations were taken.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn 5 mg tablets repackaged into opaque capsules with lactose filler), two capsules at 1000 h and two at 1800 h. In the 10 mg daily condition one active and one placebo capsule were given at each time; in the 20 mg daily condition two active capsules were given at each time. Each block ran three consecutive days (pp. 398-399).
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco was freely available except overnight and is not quantified in the analyses; caffeine, alcohol and other drugs were not available during the residential phase. Prior use of cocaine, cannabis, alcohol and caffeine was recorded at screening but not adjusted for (pp. 398-399).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential confinement for the whole 15 days, with placebo baseline days 1-3 before the first active block and placebo days between blocks; no biological verification is described. Each participant had received a single 10 mg sample dose as an outpatient before admission, so the first active day was not the first exposure (pp. 398-399).

comparison.controls: The same participants on placebo: the three baseline days (days 1-3) for the active-day comparisons, and the three placebo days after each active block for the residual-effect comparisons; each active or post-drug day was compared with the corresponding baseline day (day 1 with day 1, and so on).
comparison.matching: Within-person; the order of the two dose blocks was varied (four participants had the smaller dose first, three the larger), but allocation is not described as random.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same person's placebo baseline days.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); tobacco use continued in both conditions.

outcomes.instruments: Fifty 100-mm visual analogue scales of mood and physical state, eleven times a day; a six-item drug-effects questionnaire (good, bad and other effects rated 0-4; liking from -4 to +4; desire to take the drug again), twice a day one hour after each dose; a 45-minute performance battery nine times a day (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); continuous food and drink recording by bar code, verified against the discarded packaging, giving total calories, macronutrients, number of eating occasions, occasion size and the interval between occasions; Nightcap eye- and body-movement monitors giving sleep efficiency, movements, non-REM sleep, REM sleep and total sleep, plus six sleep visual analogue scales and an estimate of hours slept (pp. 398-399).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory instruments for this research group; the visual analogue scales have no external norms, and the Nightcap is a movement-based monitor rather than polysomnography.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a significant difference from the matched placebo baseline day on day 1 of dosing that is no longer significant by day 3, not as a tested interaction between dose and day. 'Abuse liability' is inferred from the balance of positive and negative subjective ratings and from debriefing reports.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: A modified Bonferroni rule: only planned comparisons with P below 0.01 were treated as significant. With fifty visual analogue items, six drug-effects items, five sleep measures, six sleep ratings, several food-intake measures and five performance tasks, each tested on three active days and three post-drug days at two doses, the number of comparisons is far larger than the number reported (p. 399).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants were told only that they would receive one or more commonly prescribed medications that might feel stimulant-like, sedative-like or like nothing at all, and were debriefed at discharge; capsules were identical. The paper does not state that staff were blind, and blinding integrity was not tested (p. 398).

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes and almost no printed means: the subjective, food-intake and sleep results are given as F values with P values, with the values themselves shown only in Figures 1-3 and Table 1. The quantities that are printed are the reductions in total daily intake, about 1150 kcal at 10 mg a day and about 1450 kcal at 20 mg a day relative to the placebo baseline (p. 401), and an increase of about 65 minutes in the interval between eating occasions on day 1 of the larger dose. All F values have 1 and 48 degrees of freedom.
analysis.covariates: None. Repeated-measures analyses of variance with planned comparisons on area-under-the-curve values (trapezoidal), by condition (placebo baseline, each dose, and the placebo days after each dose) and day (1, 2, 3 within each condition).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned; the study was approved by the New York State Psychiatric Institute Institutional Review Board (p. 398).
analysis.selective_reporting: Performance results are dismissed in one sentence as showing no consistent effects and are not shown; the drug-effects questionnaire results are described as 'data not shown'; macronutrient and eating-occasion-size results are partly not shown; time courses and absolute values appear only in figures without printed numbers.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation and no power statement. Seven participants, with every effect tested within person on area-under-the-curve values across three days.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 20 mg a day, ratings of 'good drug effect' and 'high' rose above the matched placebo baseline on the first day of dosing and were no longer significantly raised by day 3, while several unpleasant ratings (dizzy, flu-like symptoms, confused, depressed, nauseated, chills, unable to concentrate, bad drug effect) became significant only on day 3; ratings of 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days. At the same dose, sleep measures were disrupted on the first night only. Food intake fell by about 1150-1450 kcal a day and stayed down on all three days at both doses. The 10 mg a day condition did not differ from baseline on the positive ratings.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion describe the study as providing clear evidence of tolerance to positive subjective effects and of emerging negative effects, and conclude that the abuse liability of oral methamphetamine is relatively low in this population. The results support a loss of the positive effects across three days at the larger dose, but tolerance is inferred from a significant difference on day 1 that is absent on day 3 rather than from a tested dose-by-day interaction, the number of participants is seven, and the conclusion about abuse liability rests on ratings and debriefing in volunteers reporting minimal current stimulant use, with no self-administration or choice measure. The authors themselves attribute the difference from earlier reports to the population tested.

timeline.event: Thirteen days of daily oral methamphetamine 10 mg (slow-release) in 6 men: tolerance to the heart-rate increase but not to ratings of 'high', with a single daily dose

Three days of twice-daily oral d-amphetamine (10 mg/70 kg) in a residential laboratory from the same group: tolerance to ratings of potency, liking and stimulation by day 3, without a rise in negative ratings (Kelly, Foltin & Fischman, 1991)
Pharmacokinetics before and after 13 days of daily oral methamphetamine: no change that could explain tolerance

Three administrations of oral methamphetamine 10 mg with and without alcohol over two days in a residential laboratory: heart-rate and 'good drug effect' increases diminished by the third administration

replication.where_it_stands: Loss of the positive subjective effects of low oral methamphetamine over days of repeated dosing has now been seen in two residential studies from the same laboratory (this one and Kirkpatrick et al.) and with d-amphetamine in the same setting; the one study with a single daily dose of a slow-release preparation found no such loss on ratings of 'high' but did find it for heart rate. The emergence of unpleasant effects by day 3 rests on this study alone.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (p. 403).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University; the same laboratory produced the d-amphetamine comparison study that the discussion leans on and the later methamphetamine-alcohol study, so these are not independent replications.

what_would_settle_it: A residential study in people who use methamphetamine regularly, with the drug given at the same time each day for a week or more by a route and dose closer to non-medical use, with plasma concentrations measured, a self-administration or choice procedure beside the ratings, and a pre-specified dose-by-day interaction test rather than day-wise comparisons against baseline.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two dose blocks)
domains.note: Four participants received the smaller dose block first and three the larger, but allocation is not described as random and no sequence generation or concealment is reported.

Three placebo days separated the two active blocks, and each active day was compared with the matching baseline day; residual effects were measured and had disappeared by the second or third placebo day for most measures.

Participants were misled about the drug class and capsules were identical, but staff blinding is not stated and blinding integrity was not assessed; participants reported clear drug effects at the larger dose.
One of eight participants left because of methamphetamine-related insomnia and is not in the analyses, and 16 of 105 sleep records were imputed.

Food intake was recorded objectively and verified against discarded packaging, and sleep was measured by movement monitors; the primary outcome, however, is self-rated mood on scales whose blinding cannot be assumed.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; fifty mood items and several dozen further measures tested on six days at two doses with a P<0.01 rule; performance and drug-effects-questionnaire results are not shown; and several Table 1 entries are marked at thresholds their own F values do not reach (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A within-person residential design with its own placebo baseline days, continuous observation and objective food and sleep recording is a strong way to study repeated dosing, and the food-intake and sleep findings are measured rather than rated. The overall judgment is driven by the reported-result domain: there is no protocol, the number of comparisons is far larger than the number reported, the performance data are set aside in a sentence, and the significance markings in the main table do not all match the stated thresholds. The source can be cited for the direction and timing of the changes across three days of low oral dosing in healthy volunteers with little current stimulant use, and for the sustained fall in food intake; it cannot be cited for effects at non-medical doses or routes, for people who use methamphetamine regularly, or for precise effect sizes, which are not printed.

key_findings.finding: Ratings of 'good drug effect' and 'high' rose above the matched placebo baseline day only on the first day of the 20 mg-a-day condition (F(1,48)=8.0 and 15.0 respectively) and had returned to baseline levels by day 3, which the authors read as tolerance. Ratings in the 10 mg-a-day condition did not differ from baseline on either item.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 399, right column, continuing p. 400); Figure 1 (p. 400)
key_findings.note: The printed P values for these two F values are transposed: with 1 and 48 degrees of freedom, F=8.0 corresponds to P=0.007 and F=15.0 to P=0.0003, while the paper prints P<0.0003 for the first and P<0.007 for the second (editors' calculation from the F distribution).

key_findings.finding: Unpleasant ratings moved the other way across the three days. Dizziness (F(1,48)=9.8, P<0.003) and flu-like symptoms (F(1,48)=13.2, P<0.007) rose on the third day but not the first of the 20 mg-a-day condition, and ratings of being unable to concentrate, chills, confused, depressed and nauseated, and 'bad drug effect' on the drug-effects questionnaire (F=17.4), also became significant only on day 3.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Table 1 (p. 400)

key_findings.finding: Two unpleasant effects did not fade: 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days of the 20 mg-a-day condition (heart pounding F=16.4, 7.1 and 6.4 on days 1-3; trouble sleeping F=12.2, 13.2 and 8.8), and 'heart pounding' was also raised on day 3 of the 10 mg-a-day condition (F=11.9).

Total daily food intake fell by about 1150 kcal at 10 mg a day and about 1450 kcal at 20 mg a day relative to the placebo baseline, and the reduction was sustained on all three active days at both doses (F(1,48)=19.2, 44.4 and 29.9 on days 1-3 at the smaller dose; 62.7, 43.9 and 39.6 at the larger; all P<0.0001). Both doses also reduced protein, carbohydrate and fat intake, with no selective effect.
key_findings.locator: Results > Food intake, 1st paragraph and the sentence at the top of the right column; Figure 3 (p. 401)

key_findings.finding: The fall in intake came from fewer eating occasions (F=7.0 at the smaller dose day 1; F=12.1 at the larger) and from smaller occasions (F=19.1 and 11.6 on day 2), with the interval between eating occasions about 65 minutes longer on day 1 of the larger dose (F=7.9). Intake was still below baseline on the first placebo day after both doses (F=9.7 and 16.6) and on the third placebo day after the smaller dose (F=11.1).

Sleep was disrupted on the first night of the 20 mg-a-day condition only: total sleep time (F=12.5), total non-REM sleep (F=8.2) and sleep efficiency (F=8.1) fell and movements rose (F=15.4) against the matched baseline night, with matching falls in ratings of sleeping well, satisfaction with sleep, falling asleep easily and estimated hours slept, and a rise in waking often. Most of these effects were present on day 1 but not days 2 or 3, which the authors also read as tolerance, and no rebound was seen on the placebo days that followed.
key_findings.locator: Results > Sleep, whole section (p. 401, right column)

key_findings.finding: Ratings of hunger fell significantly (F=8.2 on day 2 of the smaller dose and 11.2 on day 1 of the larger), and the desire to take the drug again was significantly lower than baseline (F=11.2, day 2 of the smaller dose). Methamphetamine had no consistent effect on any performance task, and those data are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Data analysis, last paragraph (p. 399); Table 1, 'Hungry' and 'Desire to take drug again' rows (p. 400); Results > Food intake / drug-effects questionnaire paragraph (p. 401)

key_findings.finding: Most participants said at debriefing that they did not like the effects of methamphetamine and would not take it again outside the laboratory, attributing their dislike mainly to stomach upset and disturbed sleep; one of the eight people who started the study left because of difficulty sleeping after dosing.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods > Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 398); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 401)

reporting_issues.issue: The P values printed for the two positive subjective ratings are transposed. With 1 and 48 degrees of freedom, F=8.0 gives P=0.007 and F=15.0 gives P=0.0003, but the Results print 'good drug effect' as F(1,48)=8.0, P<0.0003 and 'high' as F(1,48)=15.0, P<0.007 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither claim changes: both comparisons are significant under the paper's own P<0.01 rule. A reader quoting the smaller P value for the wrong item would misstate the strength of the test.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 entries carry significance markers their F values do not support under the stated thresholds. The table defines * as P<0.01 and ** as P<0.005, yet with 1 and 48 degrees of freedom P<0.01 requires F of about 7.19 and P<0.005 about 8.66. Entries marked * with F=6.4 (twice), 6.5, 6.6, 6.7 and 7.1 correspond to P of about 0.015, 0.014, 0.013, 0.013 and 0.010, and the entry marked ** with F=8.6 corresponds to P of about 0.005 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Six of the negative-effect entries do not meet the paper's own modified Bonferroni rule of P<0.01, including 'anxious' on day 1, 'depressed', 'nauseated', 'noises seem loud' on day 2 and 'heart pounding' on days 2 and 3 of the larger dose. Claims should rest on the entries that clear the threshold ('trouble sleeping', 'sweating', 'jittery', 'confused', 'noises seem loud' on day 3, 'bad drug effect') and say that the day-3 picture is built from many uncorrected comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Doses are expressed in two ways without a consistent label: the title, abstract and methods give '5, 10 mg BID', while the discussion compares '5 mg BID (total daily dose of 10 mg)' with the higher condition, and the food-intake section writes 'Five and 10 mg methamphetamine significantly reduced total caloric intake'.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the food-intake sentence at face value would record a daily dose half the size of the one given. Anything citing this study should state the dose as 5 or 10 mg twice daily.

reporting_issues.issue: Every participant received a single 10 mg oral dose of methamphetamine on an outpatient basis before admission, to check for unusual reactions and to familiarize them with the drug; this is reported in the general procedures but not mentioned where tolerance is interpreted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'first day' of each dosing block was not each person's first exposure, so the measured decline is a decline from the first in-laboratory day rather than from a drug-naive state.

reporting_issues.issue: Tolerance is read from a pattern of day-wise comparisons against baseline (significant on day 1, not significant on day 3) rather than from a tested interaction between day and condition, and no means or confidence intervals for the day-1 to day-3 change are printed; the values appear only in figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the decline cannot be read from the paper, and a non-significant day-3 comparison in seven people is weak evidence that the effect has gone. The finding should be reported as a loss of a detectable effect, not as a measured percentage of tolerance.

reporting_issues.issue: The data-analysis section states that there were no consistent effects of methamphetamine on task performance and that those data will not be discussed further; drug-effects-questionnaire values, macronutrient intakes and eating-occasion sizes are also reported as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot judge the performance null result, which is the one outcome this group's earlier d-amphetamine work had found sensitive, and cannot check the questionnaire findings against the visual analogue scales.

reporting_issues.issue: Sixteen of 105 sleep records (15%) were lost to equipment failure or sensor detachment and replaced by multiple imputation, and the person who left the study did so because of methamphetamine-related insomnia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep analyses are of completers with imputed values, and the direction of both departures runs against finding sleep disruption.
